account_en: The entry in the Polish Biographical Dictionary on Antoni Prusimski (1744 to about 1806), the owner of Trąbczyn whose estates Prussia confiscated after the rising of 1794, by Jan Pachoński, a historian of the Polish Legions. It gives his family (son of Stefan, owner of Kamionna, Kolno and Trąbczyn), his seats in the Sejm, the commissions the Sejm of 1773-1775 named to settle disputes over estates, Trąbczyn among them, his part in the Kuyavian rising of 1794, the confiscation of his estates by Prussia, his exile in Venice, Paris, England and Dresden, his return in 1803 and his daughter Michalina, wife first of Józef Dąmbski and from 1809 of Stanisław Miączyński. It is a scholar's summary from the archives and literature it lists at the end; most of it is about his politics in exile, and its few words on the estates are to be held against the edition's documents.
account_de: Der Artikel des Polnischen Biographischen Wörterbuchs über Antoni Prusimski (1744 bis um 1806), den Herrn von Trąbczyn, dessen Güter Preußen nach dem Aufstand von 1794 einzog, von Jan Pachoński, einem Historiker der Polnischen Legionen. Er nennt seine Familie (Sohn Stefans, des Besitzers von Kamionna, Kolno und Trąbczyn), seine Sitze im Sejm, die Kommissionen, die der Sejm von 1773-1775 für Streitigkeiten um Güter einsetzte, darunter Trąbczyn, seinen Anteil am kujawischen Aufstand von 1794, die Einziehung seiner Güter durch Preußen, sein Exil in Venedig, Paris, England und Dresden, seine Rückkehr 1803 und seine Tochter Michalina, in erster Ehe Frau Józef Dąmbskis, ab 1809 Stanisław Miączyńskis. Es ist die Zusammenfassung eines Gelehrten aus den Archiven und der Literatur, die er am Ende nennt; das meiste betrifft seine Politik im Exil, und seine wenigen Worte über die Güter sind an den Dokumenten der Edition zu prüfen.

title: Regula processus granicialis campestris Regni Poloniae, secundum praxim moderni saeculi ad dislimitanda bona regalia, spiritualia et terrestria. Editio secunda
title_en: Rule of the Field Boundary Process of the Kingdom of Poland, according to the practice of the present age, for the delimitation of royal, ecclesiastical and noble estates. Second edition
author: Marcin Paciorkowski
published: Częstochowa: Jasna Góra press, 1776
account_en: A handbook of the procedure for settling boundaries between estates in the Kingdom of Poland, by Marcin Paciorkowski, a sworn sub-delegate of the municipal court of Opoczno, who worked such cases. Approved by the censor in 1749; this is the enlarged second edition of 1776, with the laws on boundaries, the law of 1768 among them. It explains the commissions, the boundary chamberlain, the summons, the inspection of the mounds and the decree, step by step, as the practice of the time had them. It does not name Trąbczyn, but it is the procedure of the boundary decrees of 1775 and 1782 between Trąbczyn and its neighbours. Janocki's Ianociana (1779) says the handbook is a reprint of Stanisław Lochowski's Processus iuris limitanei of 1641, which Paciorkowski printed under his own name (the sub-item Janocki (1779)); the 1776 title page itself calls the book Paciorkowski's, enlarged by the author.
account_de: Ein Handbuch des Verfahrens zur Festsetzung der Grenzen zwischen Gütern im Königreich Polen, von Marcin Paciorkowski, vereidigtem Subdelegaten des Grodgerichts Opoczno, der solche Sachen selbst führte. Vom Zensor 1749 genehmigt; dies ist die erweiterte zweite Auflage von 1776, mit den Gesetzen über die Grenzen, darunter dem Gesetz von 1768. Es erklärt die Kommissionen, den Grenzkämmerer, die Ladung, die Besichtigung der Grenzhügel und das Dekret Schritt für Schritt, wie die Praxis der Zeit sie kannte. Trąbczyn nennt es nicht, aber es ist das Verfahren der Grenzdekrete von 1775 und 1782 zwischen Trąbczyn und seinen Nachbarn. Janockis Ianociana (1779) sagt, das Handbuch sei ein Nachdruck des Processus iuris limitanei des Stanisław Lochowski von 1641, den Paciorkowski unter eigenem Namen drucken ließ (der angehängte Janocki (1779)); die Titelseite von 1776 schreibt das Buch selbst Paciorkowski zu, vom Verfasser vermehrt.

title: Friedrich Ludwig Fürst zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen. Stadterneuerer, dynamischer preußischer General, verlassener Ehemann, Schuldenmacher
title_en: Friedrich Ludwig, Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen. Urban renewer, dynamic Prussian general, deserted husband, debtor
author: Hans-Joachim Seidel
published: Ulm: Klemm+Oelschläger, 2018
account_en: A modern biography of the Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, written from the papers in the Hohenlohe Central Archive at Neuenstein, the archive of the correspondence in this edition. It covers his rebuilding of Ingelfingen, his Prussian career, his marriage and his debts, and the South Prussian estates and Triebenfeld's part in them; its appendix 6 transcribes the letter of 7 March 1809 that stands in the edition as letters 48 and 302 of Oe 1 Bü 9454. The edition's documents are the authority where the two differ (editor, 2026-10-03: primary sources before Seidel).
account_de: Eine moderne Biographie des Fürsten zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, geschrieben aus den Akten des Hohenlohe-Zentralarchivs Neuenstein, des Archivs der Korrespondenz dieser Edition. Sie behandelt seine Erneuerung Ingelfingens, seine preußische Laufbahn, seine Ehe und seine Schulden sowie die südpreußischen Güter und Triebenfelds Rolle darin; ihr Anhang 6 gibt den Brief vom 7. März 1809 wieder, der in der Edition als Briefe 48 und 302 von Oe 1 Bü 9454 steht. Wo beide abweichen, gelten die Dokumente der Edition (Herausgeber, 2026-10-03: Primärquellen vor Seidel).
summary_en:
A biography of Friedrich Ludwig, Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen (1746-1818), called "FL" throughout, by Hans-Joachim Seidel, who grew up in Ingelfingen. It is drawn above all from the letters and papers in the Hohenlohe Central Archive at Neuenstein, many of them quoted at length, from Adolf Fischer's history of the House of Hohenlohe (1871) and from Gerlinde Kraus's study of the Upper Silesian estates (2001). Twenty-three chapters, with "excursuses" on the background, eight appendices and a list of sources; the notes (pp. 257-266) are not transcribed in the edition's copy.

### Ingelfingen and the family (chapters 1-2)

The little town of Ingelfingen on the Kocher and the Ingelfingen line of the House of Hohenlohe, founded by Count Christian Kraft at the beginning of the eighteenth century; FL's father Heinrich August, who introduced primogeniture in 1774. FL is born on 31 January 1746, taught by tutors at Ingelfingen and Öhringen, and made as a boy to keep account of his pocket money, without lasting effect. In 1782 he marries Marianne, Countess Hoym zu Droyßig, seventeen years younger and a great heiress; Frederick II had pointed her out to him. Seidel lists their eight children (August, born 1784, the successor; Adelheid, Emilie, Auguste; Adolph, born 1797, later briefly Prussian minister-president; Alexander, born 1798; two who died as infants), the marriage settlements, and Marianne's mother, Princess Christiane von der Osten-Sacken, who managed the Hoym fortune. Marianne leaves husband and children in 1799. An anonymous epistolary novel of 1792 about a "Marianne von Ingelfingen" and her brutal husband is discussed and set aside. An excursus gathers what the archive holds on FL's children born outside the marriage: a son born in Berlin in 1782, a daughter of about 1775 for whom he settled a house and an annuity that later lapsed and was restored in 1806, and three children raised by a foster mother who came forward after his death.

### The Mariannenvorstadt (chapter 3)

As Hereditary Prince, from 1782, FL founded a suburb of craftsmen at Ingelfingen, named after his wife: free building land, building subsidies, ten years free of dues and of billeting, settlers chosen with care (drunkards refused, a Catholic admitted in 1787 for the sake of tolerance), houses planned by his director of buildings and salines J. G. Glenk and built in two phases to about 1806. Further plans (a jewellery factory, a river bath, a grain market, mills) mostly came to little; a Latin school, an "industrial school" (1792) and a drawing school were set up.

### The general (chapters 4-6)

FL's career: a captain in the Franconian Circle regiment at seventeen, in Prussian service from 1766, colonel, major general, inspector general in Silesia, governor of Breslau from 1791, with the King at Pillnitz in 1791. In the war against revolutionary France he led the advance guard and won at Kaiserslautern (1794). After the Peace of Basel (1795) he watched the demarcation line from Frankfurt, kept the French out of the city, which made him its first honorary citizen, and won neutrality for the Hohenlohe lands; he was close to Hardenberg. Chapter 5 gives Marianne's letters to him from Berlin in 1792 and his letters to the young children (1798-1806), among them one of 1799 asking that an enclosure be sent to the war councillor von Triebenfeld, and his letter from Dresden of September 1806 on taking command of the Prussian-Saxon army. FL became reigning Prince in 1796 with a programme for agriculture, trade and commerce, but lived at Breslau as governor: a town palace bought in 1794, and at Alt-Scheitnig a summer house and a park he opened to the public, where he received the King with illuminations and festivities. In 1805 he succeeded his childless uncle at Öhringen; in August 1806 he had his son August declared of age, handed the principality to him and resigned; Hohenlohe passed to the new Kingdom of Württemberg.

### The separation (chapter 7)

The "Transact" of 9 and 19 November 1799, drawn up by Princess Sacken for her daughter: an allowance for Marianne, Schloss Oppurg, her possessions, the provision of the children and the House, the cession of Slawentzitz in Upper Silesia to FL, and an inventory of FL's own estates, among them the South Prussian ones (the Konin estates, the Kujavian and Meseritz estates). The divorce papers of 6 August 1804, in which Marianne accepts the blame for leaving. And her "word of trust" of 12 October 1811 to her sons and the guardians, found by Kraus: she had left, she wrote, to save her children's fortune from his debts, after being made to sign for enormous sums again and again. She married Count Friedrich von der Osten-Sacken and had two daughters.

### 1806 and its judges (chapters 8-10)

FL's letters to August (1800-1805) on Breslau, careers and August's studies at Erlangen. Jena and Auerstedt, the retreat by Magdeburg in growing disorder, and the capitulation at Prenzlau on 28 October 1806, by which FL saved the lives of his men and became for ever a co-loser of 1806; his letter from captivity of 3 November; Massenbach's own account of his mistake before Prenzlau. FL is held prisoner on parole at Öhringen until the end of 1808, then made to leave Württemberg; he reaches Slawentzitz on 4 January 1809. Chapter 10 weighs his contemporaries: Friedrich von Cölln, who blamed his debts, his wife and his advisers (Triebenfeld, Grattauer, the broker Goldstecker) and his profit from the South Prussian grants, and who says Triebenfeld received eight estates valued at 51,000 thalers and sold them for 750,000; Friedrich Buchholz (1808); an unnamed officer (1831) who praised him; the memoirs of his aide-de-camp von der Marwitz (Dresden 1805, Tsar Alexander, the King's incomprehension of Prenzlau); and Goethe, whom FL met in the campaign of 1792 and at Jena in October 1806, where Goethe stopped the printing of Massenbach's manifesto against Napoleon.

### Upper Silesia, Glenck (chapters 11-12)

Slawentzitz, from the Hoym inheritance, as his seat in old age; his offer of service to the King in March 1813, declined in eight lines. His estates and works in Upper Silesia (Koschentin, bought in 1804 for 925,000 thalers, Landsberg, Bytkow, Lassowitz), farm buildings, mills, ironworks and mining with the English expert Baildon; the great wealth of "Hohenlohehütte" came only to a grandson. Chapter 12 follows the salines of Weißbach and Niedernhall and the search for coal financed by shares, with the father and son Glenk/Glenck, which failed; their letters to FL run from 1802 to 1817. The younger Glenck later found salt at Stotternheim (1828, with Goethe's interest) and in Basel-Land, and appears among FL's creditors.

### South Prussia (chapter 13)

The second and third partitions, the province of South Prussia with its chambers at Posen, Kalisch and Warsaw, and the King's settlement of German colonists on church and crown lands. The "squandering of estates": a founding board of Hoym, Bischofswerder, Triebenfeld and the King's chamberlain Ritz; Hans von Held's denunciation (1800) and the fall of Minister Hoym (1798). FL's own share, quoted from Breyer (1938): in 1796, the church estates of the lordship of Zagórów and the lordship of Trąbczyn; a hereditary lease concluded by Triebenfeld with eighteen German colonists, dated 18 May 1805 and approved by the Kalisz chamber on 28 January 1806; and the German villages named after FL's children and Hohenlohe places (Sophiental, Ludwigslust, Friedrichsfelde, Adelshof, Adolfsberg, Ingelfingen for Anielewo, Emilienheim for Michalinów, Augustinhof, Schwentz for Święcia, Kolonweiler for Wrąbczyn, Klein-Öhring), with Breyer's map. FL's correspondence with the King in 1798 about the lordship of Krotoszyn, and his help to Massenbach, who was granted Białokosz.

### The debts (chapter 14)

FL left a mountain of debt: 280,000 florins in 1806, loans from the Duke of Courland (300,000 thalers, 1790) and the Schlabrendorffs (1798), and the purchase of Koschentin. In a letter of 25 September 1806 he puts the net yield of Zagórów and Trąbczyn, confirmed by the Kalisz chamber, at 40,247 thalers and proposes to borrow 480,000 on the two estates to pay all his debts. From local accounts Seidel adds that five estates (Trąbczyn, Nowa Wieś, Osiny, Łazy, Szetlewek) were worth about 80,000 thalers and that half was sold to Weigel of Kopojno. After 1807 the Polish estates yielded nothing. Triebenfeld's letter of 14 March 1808 tells of his arrest by French gendarmes for 5,000 thalers of interest owed to the Invalids' Fund, which the banker Oppenheimer had undertaken to pay, and of Minister Zastrow's surety. Further: Triebenfeld's activity report of 7 March 1809 from Kontopp (appendix 6), the suit of the Invalids' Fund before the Kammergericht in 1811 (appendix 7), a payment owed in 1813 by a "Count Tercinoky" as owner of Zagórów, and Triebenfeld's lists of debts. Massenbach and Triebenfeld were in debt too.

### The last years and after (chapters 15-23)

The new Kingdom of Württemberg and its curbs on the mediatised princes (15). The letters of the former tutor Kahlert, 1807-1818: a press digest from Breslau on the quarrel over 1806 (the "Feuerbrände", Cölln, Massenbach, a defence of Prenzlau), then books and news (16). Marianne's letters to Cosmar (1811) and to August (1816-1817), with her troubles over a mortgage of 43,000 thalers held by Hardenberg on Bellin (17). FL's sister Sophie Christiane, who brought up the youngest children and nursed him at the end (18). The last letters to him, from the King, Kahlert, his nephew Eduard and his sons (19). FL dies at Slawentzitz on 15 February 1818; creditors come at once; the South Prussian estates are sold; Zagórów now lies in Congress Poland, and Triebenfeld seeks compensation at Vienna. Marianne dies in Mecklenburg in 1840 (20). The sons: August II, Württemberg politician and later of Slawentzitz; Adolph; Alexander (21). An excursus on Christian von Massenbach, FL's quartermaster general and contrary figure: his writings, his radical speeches in the Württemberg diet of 1817, his arrest and fortress sentence (22). A closing portrait: the loyal general of the Prussian kings, no patron of the arts, a caring father after the separation (23).

### The appendices

A table of FL's military career; a map of Upper Silesia and of Poland after the third partition; a list of his estates with their German names; Triebenfeld's statement of the debts (366,000) and a list of 1817 (among the creditors Oppenheimer and Glenck); a transcription of Triebenfeld's letter of 7 March 1809 from Kontopp, thirteen powers of attorney given for the South Prussian estates through the justice burgomaster of Zagórów (Seidel reads "Habich"; the edition's Hawich), against the sequestrator, the banker Oppenheimer, a lessee and the colonists, which stands in the edition as letters 48 and 302 of Oe 1 Bü 9454; extracts from the proceedings of 1811, in which the Invalids' Fund, having lent Triebenfeld 50,000 thalers in 1805 on the security of FL's bond of 1 June 1804 for 250,000 on the Zagórów estates, seeks to attach a legacy of 80,000 rumoured to have come to FL from Princess Sacken; and a list of the wages owed to FL's servants in 1817.

### Where the edition's documents say otherwise

The edition follows its documents. Trąbczyn, with Szetlewek, Nowa Wieś, Łazy and Osiny, came to FL by the King's deed of gift of 9 August 1796 as estates fallen to the crown, that is Prusimski's confiscated estates (Oe 1 Bü 14525, doc. 1), not as crown or starost land; Zagórów came by a deed of grant of 19 June 1797 (I. HA Rep. 162 Nr. 295, doc. 3), not in 1796. The edition's copy of the colonists' lease lacks its beginning and is dated by its engrossing, 21 March 1806 (APP 53/968/0/-/801, doc. 3), so the 18 May 1805 can be neither confirmed nor ruled out; the chamber's consent of 28 January 1806 (doc. 2) and Triebenfeld's bond of 28 January 1805 for the 50,000 thalers (Rep. 162 Nr. 295, doc. 1) agree.
summary_de:
Eine Biographie Friedrich Ludwigs, Fürst zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen (1746-1818), im Buch durchgehend „FL“, von Hans-Joachim Seidel, der in Ingelfingen aufwuchs. Sie schöpft vor allem aus den Briefen und Akten des Hohenlohe-Zentralarchivs Neuenstein, die oft ausführlich angeführt werden, aus Adolf Fischers Geschichte des Hauses Hohenlohe (1871) und aus der Untersuchung der oberschlesischen Güter von Gerlinde Kraus (2001). Dreiundzwanzig Kapitel mit „Exkursen“ zum Hintergrund, acht Anhänge und ein Quellenverzeichnis; die Anmerkungen (S. 257-266) sind in der Abschrift der Edition nicht übertragen.

### Ingelfingen und die Familie (Kapitel 1-2)

Das Städtchen Ingelfingen am Kocher und die Ingelfinger Linie des Hauses Hohenlohe, Anfang des 18. Jahrhunderts von Graf Christian Kraft begründet; FLs Vater Heinrich August, der 1774 die Erstgeburt einführte. FL wird am 31. Januar 1746 geboren, von Hauslehrern in Ingelfingen und Öhringen unterrichtet und muss schon als Knabe über sein Taschengeld Buch führen, ohne bleibende Wirkung. 1782 heiratet er Marianne, Gräfin Hoym zu Droyßig, siebzehn Jahre jünger und eine reiche Erbin, auf die ihn Friedrich II. hingewiesen hatte. Seidel nennt die acht Kinder (August, geb. 1784, der Nachfolger; Adelheid, Emilie, Auguste; Adolph, geb. 1797, später kurz preußischer Ministerpräsident; Alexander, geb. 1798; zwei als Säuglinge gestorben), die Eheverträge und Mariannes Mutter, Fürstin Christiane von der Osten-Sacken, die das Hoymsche Vermögen verwaltete. 1799 verlässt Marianne Mann und Kinder. Ein anonymer Briefroman von 1792 über eine „Marianne von Ingelfingen“ und ihren rohen Gatten wird erörtert und beiseitegelegt. Ein Exkurs sammelt, was das Archiv über FLs außereheliche Kinder enthält: einen 1782 in Berlin geborenen Sohn, eine Tochter von etwa 1775, der er ein Haus und eine Rente aussetzte, die später ausblieb und 1806 wieder gezahlt wurde, und drei von einer Pflegemutter aufgezogene Kinder, die sich nach seinem Tod meldete.

### Die Mariannenvorstadt (Kapitel 3)

Als Erbprinz gründete FL ab 1782 in Ingelfingen eine Vorstadt für Handwerker, nach seiner Frau benannt: freier Bauplatz, Baukostenzuschüsse, zehn Jahre frei von Abgaben und Einquartierung, sorgfältig ausgewählte Siedler (Trinker abgewiesen, 1787 um der Toleranz willen ein Katholik aufgenommen), die Häuser von seinem Bau- und Salinendirektor J. G. Glenk geplant und in zwei Abschnitten bis um 1806 gebaut. Weitere Pläne (eine Bijouteriefabrik, ein Flussbad, ein Kornmarkt, Mühlen) blieben meist liegen; eine Lateinschule, eine „Industrieschule“ (1792) und eine Zeichenschule entstanden.

### Der General (Kapitel 4-6)

FLs Laufbahn: mit siebzehn Hauptmann im Fränkischen Kreisregiment, seit 1766 in preußischem Dienst, Oberst, Generalmajor, Generalinspekteur in Schlesien, seit 1791 Gouverneur von Breslau, 1791 mit dem König in Pillnitz. Im Krieg gegen das revolutionäre Frankreich führte er die Vorhut und siegte bei Kaiserslautern (1794). Nach dem Basler Frieden (1795) überwachte er von Frankfurt aus die Demarkationslinie, hielt die Franzosen von der Stadt fern, die ihn dafür zu ihrem ersten Ehrenbürger machte, und erreichte die Neutralität der hohenlohischen Lande; er stand Hardenberg nahe. Kapitel 5 bringt Mariannes Briefe an ihn aus Berlin von 1792 und seine Briefe an die jungen Kinder (1798-1806), darunter einen von 1799 mit der Bitte, eine Beilage an den Kriegsrat von Triebenfeld zu senden, und seinen Brief aus Dresden vom September 1806 über die Übernahme des Befehls über die preußisch-sächsische Armee. 1796 wurde FL regierender Fürst, mit einem Programm für Landwirtschaft, Gewerbe und Handel, lebte aber als Gouverneur in Breslau: ein 1794 gekauftes Stadtpalais und in Alt-Scheitnig ein Sommerhaus mit einem Park, den er der Öffentlichkeit öffnete und wo er den König mit Illuminationen und Festen empfing. 1805 folgte er seinem kinderlosen Onkel in Öhringen; im August 1806 ließ er seinen Sohn August für volljährig erklären, übergab ihm das Fürstentum und dankte ab; Hohenlohe fiel an das neue Königreich Württemberg.

### Die Trennung (Kapitel 7)

Der „Transact“ vom 9. und 19. November 1799, von Fürstin Sacken für ihre Tochter aufgesetzt: ein Unterhalt für Marianne, Schloss Oppurg, ihre Habe, die Versorgung der Kinder und des Hauses, die Abtretung von Slawentzitz in Oberschlesien an FL und ein Verzeichnis von FLs eigenen Gütern, darunter die südpreußischen (die Koniner Güter, die kujawischen und Meseritzer Güter). Die Scheidungspapiere vom 6. August 1804, in denen Marianne die Schuld am Weggehen auf sich nimmt. Und ihr „Wort des Vertrauens“ vom 12. Oktober 1811 an ihre Söhne und die Vormünder, von Kraus gefunden: Sie sei gegangen, um das Vermögen der Kinder vor seinen Schulden zu retten, nachdem sie immer wieder für ungeheure Summen habe unterschreiben müssen. Sie heiratete Graf Friedrich von der Osten-Sacken und bekam zwei Töchter.

### 1806 und seine Richter (Kapitel 8-10)

FLs Briefe an August (1800-1805) über Breslau, Laufbahnen und Augusts Studium in Erlangen. Jena und Auerstedt, der Rückzug über Magdeburg in wachsender Unordnung und die Kapitulation von Prenzlau am 28. Oktober 1806, mit der FL seinen Leuten das Leben rettete und für immer ein Mitverlierer von 1806 wurde; sein Brief aus der Gefangenschaft vom 3. November; Massenbachs eigener Bericht über seinen Irrtum vor Prenzlau. FL bleibt bis Ende 1808 auf Ehrenwort Gefangener in Öhringen, muss dann Württemberg verlassen und erreicht am 4. Januar 1809 Slawentzitz. Kapitel 10 wägt die Zeitgenossen: Friedrich von Cölln, der seine Schulden, seine Frau, seine Berater (Triebenfeld, Grattauer, den Makler Goldstecker) und seinen Gewinn aus den südpreußischen Schenkungen tadelte und schreibt, Triebenfeld habe acht Güter im Schätzwert von 51.000 Talern erhalten und für 750.000 verkauft; Friedrich Buchholz (1808); ein ungenannter Offizier (1831), der ihn rühmte; die Erinnerungen seines Adjutanten von der Marwitz (Dresden 1805, Zar Alexander, das Unverständnis des Königs für Prenzlau); und Goethe, dem FL im Feldzug von 1792 und im Oktober 1806 in Jena begegnete, wo Goethe den Druck von Massenbachs Manifest gegen Napoleon verhinderte.

### Oberschlesien, Glenck (Kapitel 11-12)

Slawentzitz aus dem Hoymschen Erbe als Alterssitz; sein Dienstangebot an den König vom März 1813, in acht Zeilen abgelehnt. Seine Güter und Werke in Oberschlesien (Koschentin, 1804 für 925.000 Taler gekauft, Landsberg, Bytkow, Lassowitz), Wirtschaftsgebäude, Mühlen, Eisenwerke und Bergbau mit dem englischen Fachmann Baildon; den großen Reichtum der „Hohenlohehütte“ erlangte erst ein Enkel. Kapitel 12 verfolgt die Salinen von Weißbach und Niedernhall und die mit Aktien finanzierte Suche nach Kohle mit Vater und Sohn Glenk/Glenck, die scheiterte; ihre Briefe an FL reichen von 1802 bis 1817. Der jüngere Glenck fand später Salz bei Stotternheim (1828, unter Goethes Anteilnahme) und in Basel-Land und erscheint unter FLs Gläubigern.

### Südpreußen (Kapitel 13)

Die zweite und dritte Teilung, die Provinz Südpreußen mit ihren Kammern in Posen, Kalisch und Warschau und die Ansiedlung deutscher Kolonisten auf geistlichen und Krongütern. Die „Güterverschleuderung“: ein Gründungsgremium aus Hoym, Bischofswerder, Triebenfeld und dem königlichen Kämmerier Ritz; Hans von Helds Anklage (1800) und der Sturz Minister Hoyms (1798). FLs eigener Anteil, nach Breyer (1938): 1796 die geistlichen Güter der Herrschaft Zagórów und die Herrschaft Trąbczyn; ein von Triebenfeld mit achtzehn deutschen Kolonisten geschlossener Erbpachtvertrag vom 18. Mai 1805, von der Kalischer Kammer am 28. Januar 1806 genehmigt; und die nach FLs Kindern und hohenlohischen Orten benannten deutschen Dörfer (Sophiental, Ludwigslust, Friedrichsfelde, Adelshof, Adolfsberg, Ingelfingen für Anielewo, Emilienheim für Michalinów, Augustinhof, Schwentz für Święcia, Kolonweiler für Wrąbczyn, Klein-Öhring), mit Breyers Karte. FLs Briefwechsel mit dem König 1798 über die Herrschaft Krotoszyn und seine Hilfe für Massenbach, der Białokosz erhielt.

### Die Schulden (Kapitel 14)

FL hinterließ einen Schuldenberg: 280.000 Gulden im Jahr 1806, Darlehen des Herzogs von Kurland (300.000 Taler, 1790) und der Schlabrendorffs (1798) und den Kauf von Koschentin. In einem Brief vom 25. September 1806 beziffert er den von der Kalischer Kammer bestätigten Reinertrag von Zagórów und Trąbczyn auf 40.247 Taler und schlägt vor, auf die beiden Güter 480.000 aufzunehmen, um alle Schulden zu bezahlen. Nach örtlichen Darstellungen ergänzt Seidel, fünf Güter (Trąbczyn, Nowa Wieś, Osiny, Łazy, Szetlewek) seien etwa 80.000 Taler wert gewesen und die Hälfte sei an Weigel von Kopojno verkauft worden. Nach 1807 brachten die polnischen Güter nichts mehr ein. Triebenfelds Brief vom 14. März 1808 berichtet von seiner Verhaftung durch französische Gendarmen wegen 5.000 Taler Zinsen an die Invalidenkasse, deren Zahlung der Bankier Oppenheimer übernommen hatte, und von Minister Zastrows Bürgschaft. Ferner: Triebenfelds Tätigkeitsbericht vom 7. März 1809 aus Kontopp (Anhang 6), die Klage der Invalidenkasse vor dem Kammergericht 1811 (Anhang 7), eine 1813 von einem „Grafen Tercinoky“ als Besitzer von Zagórów geschuldete Zahlung und Triebenfelds Schuldenlisten. Auch Massenbach und Triebenfeld waren verschuldet.

### Die letzten Jahre und danach (Kapitel 15-23)

Das neue Königreich Württemberg und seine Beschränkungen der mediatisierten Fürsten (15). Die Briefe des einstigen Hauslehrers Kahlert 1807-1818: eine Presseschau aus Breslau zum Streit über 1806 (die „Feuerbrände“, Cölln, Massenbach, eine Verteidigung von Prenzlau), dann Bücher und Neuigkeiten (16). Mariannes Briefe an Cosmar (1811) und an August (1816-1817), mit ihren Sorgen um eine Hypothek von 43.000 Talern Hardenbergs auf Bellin (17). FLs Schwester Sophie Christiane, die die jüngsten Kinder erzog und ihn am Ende pflegte (18). Die letzten Briefe an ihn, vom König, von Kahlert, seinem Neffen Eduard und seinen Söhnen (19). FL stirbt am 15. Februar 1818 in Slawentzitz; sogleich kommen die Gläubiger; die südpreußischen Güter werden verkauft; Zagórów liegt nun in Kongresspolen, und Triebenfeld sucht in Wien eine Entschädigung. Marianne stirbt 1840 in Mecklenburg (20). Die Söhne: August II., württembergischer Politiker und später in Slawentzitz; Adolph; Alexander (21). Ein Exkurs über Christian von Massenbach, FLs Generalquartiermeister und Gegenfigur: seine Schriften, seine radikalen Reden im württembergischen Landtag 1817, seine Verhaftung und Festungsstrafe (22). Ein abschließendes Bild: der treue General der preußischen Könige, kein Förderer der Künste, ein fürsorglicher Vater nach der Trennung (23).

### Die Anhänge

Eine Tafel von FLs militärischer Laufbahn; eine Karte Oberschlesiens und Polens nach der dritten Teilung; ein Verzeichnis seiner Güter mit ihren deutschen Namen; Triebenfelds Aufstellung der Schulden (366.000) und eine Liste von 1817 (unter den Gläubigern Oppenheimer und Glenck); eine Übertragung von Triebenfelds Brief vom 7. März 1809 aus Kontopp, dreizehn Vollmachten für die südpreußischen Güter über den Justizbürgermeister von Zagórów (bei Seidel „Habich“, in der Edition Hawich), gegen den Sequester, den Bankier Oppenheimer, einen Pächter und die Kolonisten, der in der Edition als Briefe 48 und 302 von Oe 1 Bü 9454 steht; Auszüge aus dem Verfahren von 1811, in dem die Invalidenkasse, die Triebenfeld 1805 50.000 Taler auf FLs Schuldschein vom 1. Juni 1804 über 250.000 auf die Güter von Zagórów geliehen hatte, ein Vermächtnis von 80.000 mit Arrest belegen will, das FL angeblich von Fürstin Sacken zugefallen war; und eine Liste der 1817 geschuldeten Löhne von FLs Dienerschaft.

### Wo die Dokumente der Edition anderes sagen

Die Edition folgt ihren Dokumenten. Trąbczyn kam mit Szetlewek, Nowa Wieś, Łazy und Osiny durch die königliche Schenkungsurkunde vom 9. August 1796 an FL, als der Krone heimgefallene, also Prusimskis eingezogene Güter (Oe 1 Bü 14525, Dok. 1), nicht als Kron- oder Starosteigut; Zagórów kam durch eine Verleihungsurkunde vom 19. Juni 1797 (I. HA Rep. 162 Nr. 295, Dok. 3), nicht 1796. Der Abschrift des Kolonistenvertrags in der Edition fehlt der Anfang; sie ist nach ihrer Ausfertigung datiert, 21. März 1806 (APP 53/968/0/-/801, Dok. 3), sodass der 18. Mai 1805 weder bestätigt noch ausgeschlossen werden kann; die Zustimmung der Kammer vom 28. Januar 1806 (Dok. 2) und Triebenfelds Schuldschein vom 28. Januar 1805 über die 50.000 Taler (Rep. 162 Nr. 295, Dok. 1) stimmen überein.

title: Przeżyć tę jedną zimę. Listy żołnierza Wehrmachtu odkryte w ścianie domu kantora
title_en: To Survive This One Winter. The Wehrmacht Soldier's Letters Discovered in the Wall of the Cantor's House
author: Mirosław Słowiński
published: Konin: Wydawnictwo Setidava, Miejska Biblioteka Publiczna im. Zofii Urbanowskiej w Koninie, 2023 (ze Stowarzyszeniem Współpraca Polska-Wschód). ISBN 978-83-67258-15-9, ISBN 978-83-63554-53-8
account_en: A small regional book by Mirosław Słowiński (the author of Zagórów. Album miasta, 2007, and co-editor of Dwa życia jak dwa psalmy, 2012, and of Zerwane ogniwo. Ewangelicy na ziemi zagórowskiej, 2024), published by the press of the Zofia Urbanowska Public Library at Konin with the Stowarzyszenie Współpraca Polska-Wschód, and read in manuscript by Professor Artur Kijas at the author's request. It edits and discusses a hoard of letters found in 1995 walled up in the former cantor's house at Łazińsk: the correspondence of Bruno Edwin Mielke, a Wehrmacht private from Łazińsk who served on the Arctic front (the Eismeerfront at Petsamo/ Pieczenga) from 1942 to 1944, and of his family at home, written from 14 February 1940 to 14 May 1944. The letters are given translated into Polish (by a team of six, Jacek Kin foremost; the originals are kept in the archive of the MGOK at Zagórów), the commentary is the author's, an introduction sets the letters in the history of the German settlement around Zagórów, and an appendix reprints a German-era note on Łazińsk (Der Heimatbote 1981), a contemporary note, the list of the hoard's contents and the list of the cantor's library. A witness of the twentieth century, the era of the Ostdeutscher Beobachter's feature on Łazińsk of 19 July 1942 and of Breyer's Łazińsk notebook of 1936 (APP 53/968/0/-/669): its cantor Gustav Adolf Mielke - the teacher and farmer Mielke of the 1942 article, "since 1925" in Breyer's notebook - is the one man (the editor's ruling of 2026-10-22).
account_de: Ein kleines regionales Buch von Mirosław Słowiński (dem Verfasser von Zagórów. Album miasta, 2007, und Mitherausgeber von Dwa życia jak dwa psalmy, 2012, und Zerwane ogniwo. Ewangelicy na ziemi zagórowskiej, 2024), im Verlag der Zofia-Urbanowska-Stadtbibliothek zu Konin mit dem Stowarzyszenie Współpraca Polska-Wschód erschienen, vom Professor Artur Kijas auf des Verfassers Bitte in der Reinschrift gelesen. Es ediert und erörtert einen 1995 in der ehemaligen Kantorenwohnung von Łazińsk eingemauerten Bestand von Briefen: die Korrespondenz des Bruno Edwin Mielke, eines einfachen Soldaten der Wehrmacht aus Łazińsk, der von 1942 bis 1944 an der Eismeerfront bei Petsamo/Pieczenga diente, und seiner Familie in der Heimat, geschrieben vom 14. Februar 1940 bis zum 14. Mai 1944. Die Briefe sind ins Polnische übersetzt gegeben (von einem Team von sechs, an der Spitze Jacek Kin; die Originale liegen im Archiv des MGOK in Zagórów), der Kommentar ist des Verfassers, eine Einleitung ordnet die Briefe in die Geschichte der deutschen Besiedlung um Zagórów ein, und ein Anhang druckt eine Notiz der deutschen Zeit über Łazińsk nach (Der Heimatbote 1981), eine heutige Notiz, das Verzeichnis des Bestands und das Verzeichnis der Kantorbücherei. Ein Zeuge des zwanzigsten Jahrhunderts, der Zeit des Features des Ostdeutschen Beobachters über Łazińsk vom 19. Juli 1942 und des Łazińsker Notizbuchs Breyers von 1936 (APP 53/968/0/-/669): sein Kantor Gustav Adolf Mielke - der Lehrer und Bauer Mielke des Artikels von 1942, "seit 1925" im Notizbuch Breyers - ist derselbe Mann (Herausgeberentscheidung vom 22.10.2026).
summary_en:
A book of 96 PDF pages (printed pp. 7-101 and unnumbered leaves) by Mirosław Słowiński, Konin 2023, with the epigraph "Manuscripts do not burn" - Woland's word from Bulgakov's Master and Margarita. It edits a wall cache of letters found in the former cantor's house at Łazińsk and discusses them from the position of a regional historian; Scripture epigraphs from the Warsaw Bible of 1975 head each group of the letters (Psalm 25:4, 146:2, 18:36, 17:5, 71:1 among them). Twenty-five photographs of German soldiers under Petsamo/Pieczenga, from public-domain veteran archives of the Alpine countries, stand between the pages; their authors could not be traced.

### The introduction: the Germans of the Zagórów land

The letters came to light in 1995, when Bogdan Karaszewski, who had been given one of the four teachers' flats made in the former cantor's house in 1945, took down an inside door with its frame and found, in the space between two walls everyone had taken for one, a tightly wrapped bundle: letters with Wehrmacht field-post stamps, a baptism book (the Taufe of the kantorat of Łazińsk, covering 1912 to 1918, kept by the cantor of the time, E. Cellmer), altar cloths, carpentry tools - and, sliding down from above, thirty-one books, the first a biography of Joseph Goebbels. Karaszewski kept the hoard boxed for nearly twenty-five years and handed it over whole in October 2020 to the Dom Kultury at Zagórów (its director Łukasz Parus), which had announced a search for materials on the region's Protestants.

The introduction sets the story in place and time. In 1718 fourteen German families come from Silesia into eastern Wielkopolska near Zagórów; the lord of the manor of Trąbczyn leases them forest land and fallows in perpetuity, and the village of Łazińsk rises. (The book's form of the family's name is "Prusińscy"; the edition writes Prusimscy.) In 1746 the owners of the Trąbczyn estates, Katarzyna and Paweł Prusińscy, mark out further settlements, held under Olęder law: Evangelicals, free people, with their own self-government; in the last of the villages located by the heirs of Trąbczyn there were also Polish Catholic peasants. From 1746 to 1789 the heirs of neighbouring Łukomia likewise mark out new locations. "Olęder" was the name of the law, not of a nationality: it was brought to the Commonwealth by Mennonites fleeing the Netherlands, and the Warsaw Confederation of January 1573 is named as its legal guarantee. Following Zbigniew Chodyła, the book counts 637 Olęder settlements founded in Wielkopolska from 1721 to 1793/1795, of them 228 in the Kalisz voivodeship, and says the Dutch and their descendants were about one per cent of the settlers under that law. Peasants from Prussia settle in the ring of villages around Zagórów, Łazińsk the oldest and largest German-speaking settlement. After the Congress of Vienna the land lies in the Russian Kingdom of Poland; Poles, Jews and Germans live for a century and more side by side without mixed marriages or conversions, the children of the Germans and the Jews taught only their Bible and Talmud. From 1918 the well-to-do German and Jewish families and the pastors from the Reich leave for Germany; the German settlers, bound by language and religion, had literally hewn their place out of the forests below Zagórów, and when they travelled to Prussia they thought they were going on a visit. Then the Reich's agitation, the preaching of Mitteleuropa, the reports of the Konin police that only the Hakata Germans and the Bund Jews were hostile to the Polish state - and the letters' own witness that in 1939 many of the minority stood to fight the invaders in the Wehrmacht's uniform. Of the German teacher Gustav Tonn of Płatkownica's letter to Bruno Mielke of 15 July 1936 - "do not flaunt your Germandom... if Poland is to be our homeland and is, we must also be patriotically minded towards Poland" - the book asks how such counsel stood against the aggressive nationalist and Nazi propaganda then being carried among the German minority. One theme is absent from the whole war correspondence: from September to 15 November 1941 the Zagórów ghetto was liquidated and its Jews carried off to the woods near Kazimierz Biskupim to be murdered, "as if the thousand Jews, neighbours of two hundred years, had never been here at all."

The cantor's house itself: the first brick building stood at Łazińsk in 1839, and "a hundred years later" the community, whose works the cantor Gustav Adolf Mielke had directed since 1925, put up the new building with classrooms, an office and the dwelling of the schoolmaster and cantor in one. (The 1942 newspaper feature and the annex's German-era note date the new school to 1933; the introduction's "a hundred years later" is the book's own reading - NEEDS_CONFIRMATION.) Mielke was an active propagandist of the German nationalists and of Nazi propaganda, was made to leave Łazińsk in 1936 and settle somewhere in Galicia, and returned with the Wehrmacht in 1939; through the war the school, the kantorat shorn of its rights and the Mielke family lived in the building. On 18 January 1945 the Russians came; in April every German farmer was expropriated, told by some that it was a temporary measure; the house was converted into flats for teachers. From 1993 German-registered cars began to appear at Łazińsk and the nearby Kopczyk, their passengers documenting the old farmsteads, sometimes to the point of the police being called.

The hiding place itself: the end of 1944, the eastern wind and the coming front; probably one of the elder sisters, Leokadia, was at home. The cache was prepared with time, technical skill and ingenuity - most likely filled from above, from the attic, and the gap plugged. The hoard held letters from the front of the younger son Julius Samuel Mielke - Bruno - and letters and cards from the father, the brother Gustav and the sisters Leokadia (Kadzia), Anni and Olga to Bruno, besides many loose letters, postcards and documents of 1936-1939 (among them the permit of the starosta of Konin of 26 September 1939 for Gustav Adolf Mielke to move freely about the Konin powiat and to use a bicycle). How letters from home sent to the front came to be back at Łazińsk is not known - perhaps Bruno left them there on leave; the baptism book of 1912-1918 survived.

The library walled up with the letters speaks for the household: Wilfrid Bade's biography of Goebbels (Lübeck 1938), Hans Wendt on the Potsdam National Assembly of 21-23 March 1933, Treitschke's Deutsche Geschichte im 19. Jahrhundert with an introduction by Alfred Rosenberg, Walther Gehl's Der deutsche Aufbruch, Bruno Behm's Deutsche Haltung vor Fremden (the last a Tornisterschrift of the OKW), Bidez's Julian the Apostate, Ranke's Geschichte Wallenstein, a life of Frederick William IV, Raabe's Chronik der Sperlingsgasse, the Bible of Vienna 1886 - the wedding present of 14/26 June 1892 to Samuel Julius Mielke and Natalie Tonn, with its handwritten family chronicle - two collections of sermons, guides to marriage and sexual life, songbooks, and Schlag nach über England. Of the authors: Gehl killed in June 1942 on the Eastern Front; Behm of the extreme Austrian right; Treitschke's essay of 1879 and its adoption as the Stürmer's motto ("Die Juden sind unser Unglück"); Rosenberg's Myth of the Twentieth Century beside Mein Kampf, a million copies sold to 1944. Bade, the biographer, government councillor in the ministry of propaganda, died in December 1945 in Soviet captivity at Kovno; but the book's interest is the hero of the biography: Goebbels himself, his doctorate at Heidelberg (1922), his fanatical service, his oratory - a figure that must have made a deep impression on the well-read household of the cantor's house. Why the cache was made at all - fear for the letters of son and brother, fear for the books that constituted the family's national-socialist identity, hope of return - the book leaves open, asking whether the preserving of Rosenberg and Goebbels shows that the terrible defeat had taught the expellees nothing.

### The letters, 1940-1944

Bruno Edwin Mielke was born on 8 September 1911 at Białołęka, the ninth of ten children of Samuel Julius Mielke and Natalie née Tonn (married 14/26 June 1892 at Pułtusk; the children's names and birth years recorded in the family chronicle of the wedding Bible: Emil Leonhard 1893, Leokadia 1895, Florentina Amalie 1897, Gustav Adolf 1899, Olga Johanna 1901, Apolonia Dorota 1905, Hugo Georg 1906, Oswald Julius 1909, Bruno Edwin 1911, Jerene Anna Natalie 1914). He passed out of the State Teachers' Seminary with German as the language of instruction at Łódź on 28 June 1932 - "the State German Teachers' Seminary at Łódź", as he wrote in 1940, a loss of Poland from the pre-war biographies the book marks. For five years he helped Alexander Gross, the pastor of the Evangelical-Augsburg parish at Zagórów, and worked as teacher and cantor at nearby Anielewo; he taught at Konary in the gmina of Grodziec and signed a document of 1940 as teacher and junior school commissioner at Maślaki in the gmina of Wilczyn; both villages, like Łazińsk, settlements of German Protestant colonists contracted by Polish lords since the end of the eighteenth century. His dream, running through the letters, was to study at the Evangelical-Theological Faculty of the University of Vienna ("I have a teacher's training, also in music, but I know no foreign language except Polish... I am no genius, but, as the late director wrote on my certificate, I am diligent"); the letter to the dean of 10 October 1941 asks to be admitted when the war releases him, and says that if he falls, his brother will inform the dean.

The hoard's letters to the sisters run from 1940: the Lehmann family of Dresden thanking sister Flora for a parcel two days after 22 June 1941 and thanking "our dear Führer that he attacked in good time"; Bruno cramming Latin "for Vienna" on 8 July 1941, the antichrist to blame that he cannot be a teacher, his comrade Rentz fallen; the register of 28 April 1942 at the commune office with Gustav, Mundt, Grunwald, Schmechel and Stolp. Gustav's long letter of 1 May 1942 misses his brother at the school desk, is lonely ("Apart from you I have no one; our girls themselves need support, and father... sleeps and eats and reads all day; but he is well"), announces his resolve to marry, and sends food with the brotherly warning not to share it all away. On 30 May 1942 Bruno writes from Innsbruck that the training in the Alps is ending and the next day they move to Lapland - the 2nd Gebirgs Division, formed on 1 April 1938 from the Austrian 6th division, is to be the form of his war.

The letters of the northern front, from June 1942: the march ("By God's grace we reached Finland safely... two days by train and we found ourselves near a small town close by the Arctic Circle... a march that is to last many weeks"), the arrival report (about 300 km at up to 35 km a day, marching at night in the land without night, "the sun bends to the horizon, stays there, and after midnight rises majestically again"; the last 15 km by lorry with the other lame ones), the borrowed postal code and the smallness of the parcels (up to 100 g), the request for little biscuits baked of flour and dried - and, on the margin, that it is good to know Russian, for interpreters with an officer's rank have a much lighter life. The book sets this in the campaign: Finland's agreement with the Reich of October 1940, its alliance of May 1941, its declaration of war of 25 June, Operation Silberfuchs under General Dietl, the object Murmansk and the railway; the failed attack stopped by 17 July 1941, the nickel mines, the Führer's order of 22 September to break off, the Russian pilot's destruction of the bridge at Parkkino on 28 September - where Mielke's company was stationed a few kilometres from Petsamo, the front stabilized on this stretch until September 1944. (The note 20 records the present cemetery at Pieczenga: "Unseren 12 000 Toten Kameraden", built 2000-2001 by the veterans of the Alpine countries, with EISMEERFRONT 1941-1944 on a separate tablet.)

The family's July letters carry the northern front home: Gustav from Zagórów (22 July 1942), sister Anna and her fiancé Hans at the Łazińsk house, many Łazińsk men on leave from garrisons in Germany and France, the request for a photograph in uniform. Two letters of the father survive: that of 20 April 1942, written on the Führer's birthday and dedicated to him ("May the Lord God keep him in good health for a long time, until he has overcome all evil and we can sing with him the great Hallelujah of peace"), troubled that many of the locals avoid the church; and that of 28 July 1942 offering himself as a Russian interpreter, telling of the late wet harvest, and ending "Jesus makes miracles. Heil Hitler!". The letters of Olga and her husband Erwin thank Bruno for money sent and for shielding the homeland with his body; their little son is christened Adolf, the baptism modest and at home, the pastor's speech fine, the godparents Gustav and Leokadia. Anna's letters (22 September 1942 and later) are the morale the book dwells on: pride in the decisive fight, "when you return you will certainly be another man; conquer yourself", and her own plainness against his mysticism.

Bruno's long letter of 2 August 1942 to Gustav answers none of these (it probably crossed them in the post, or came back with Bruno's baggage): the move to the front on 22 August, the food (750 g of bread a day, on Sundays a third of a bar of chocolate and a fifth of a litre of schnapps), the old front soldiers' tales of the previous winter on the northern front, the preparations already being made in summer - and the sentence that gives the book its title: "My hope and prayer is to survive this one winter, and if God grants the grace of victory again, my hope is not empty. In any case it is beautiful that one of us takes part in this, and for me it is an obvious duty, even if I, with my 31 years, do not entirely understand it! Would you believe that I already feel it?" The book weighs the sentence at length: pride, or the question rising from the subconscious what he is taking part in; the greater enemy is nature; the private who has not yet met the war machine that grinds human flesh. The same letter carries his pastoral vocation ("if I return safe and well, I shall prepare myself for the most beautiful of professions... to carry it out with the greatest blessing; my heart is full of longing for a life dedicated to God - and as a pastor I can do it best of all"), his conditions for a wife (she must belong to the Saviour and be pious), and his advice to Gustav about Truthilde ("watch her and talk thoroughly with her, how far she is sanctified by Christ") - Gustav, 43, the cantor, teacher and schoolmaster of Łazińsk since 1925, still seeking a wife, and Bruno's counsel unvarying: she must be a deeply believing soul, and it would be good if she were not plain.

The pastor Gross writes from Zagórów on 13 October 1942 of the intercessory prayer held at Łazińsk on 27 September and of the Sunday prayers for the men at the distant front. The December letters bear "Eastern Front": Bruno chooses to be at the front for Christmas as a small offering for his family and people ("the days of the feast I shall not spend in sadness; that is God's will and my superiors sent me to the front"), owns his stretch is a quiet one, describes the watch of six to eight hours, the food and firewood carried, the sleeping, the late newspapers - and asks Gustav not to petition for his release: at the front in winter it is better than the training and drill of the rear. The book sets this against Stalingrad, whose decisive phase the December of 1942 was, and against the silence of the propaganda; Bruno asks for the Führer's speech of 1 October and clippings of the speeches of Goebbels, Göring and Ribbentrop, and plans his correspondence with prospective wives. The Christmas parcel from home (a three-kilogram parcel with a fir wreath with an angel's head and lametta, fixed to a locker made of an empty grenade box, colleagues given a bite to taste), the Wehrmacht's own Christmas parcels (snuff, cigarettes, sweets, chocolate, darning wool, envelopes, a comb, a bottle of vodka and of wine), the lice ointment that works ("I washed on Saturday, smeared myself all over and put on fresh linen; now no louse bites"), the day reversed by the polar night (dinner at six in the evening, supper at three in the night, breakfast at one in the afternoon), and the promotion to Oberschütze of 1 December 1942 after eight months of service, read out at his post in the presence of the enemy by Captain Lebech and Lieutenant Hensler - before which the captain asked Mielke what class of the nationality list he belonged to: the Volksliste. The Polish school year's letters come: Anna Steinbart of Konary, his successor at the school ("I shall probably not be your successor much longer"), the director of the Łódź seminary Erich Kunitzer with his son Friedrich fighting in the Kalmyk steppe and "I too would rather die at the front than fall under the rule of the Jews"; and Gustav's December letter, summoned to the education office at Konin, sworn in as a tenured official, "a teacher of the Führer", with its cold closing news: "Again and again come word that some of Łazińsk or the neighbourhood have fallen on the Eastern Front. The fighting is not easy. Not a few of them die."

The New Year's letters of January 1943: Bruno's short letter of 20 December received on 5 January (the shell that struck his main post while he prayed, "by mistake", in the side bunker); the birthday parcel; Bruno's anxiety of 10 January for his sister's soul - her fiancé Hans "rejects the teaching of Scripture and wants to protect you from such things", and Bruno means to give them a Bible as a wedding present and will not come to the wedding; Anna's steady answer ("If I left Hans for your sakes I should gain nothing... he loves me too much to force me into anything; am I to wait for a pastor, who may more than once have been insincere? I do not want to be forty or more like my sisters... he is at least loyal and trustworthy, and in no case an unbeliever"), and her warning against his religious mysticism ("you think you are no dreamer, but I think you are not far from it; forgive me if I give you pain"). Bruno's letter of 20 January on his New Year's Eve ("at ten I could vanish behind one of the snowed-up hills and receive the year 1943 praying, from God's hand") and his heavy brotherly counsel to Gustav, who carries some great burden between himself and God: go to the pastor, "he will summon the wonderful divine power (which Christ hands on with the office) and name the sin by name". The book reads in this the zeal of the future pastor for the religious formation of his siblings, and asks whether the kantorat's bans (no baptisms, funerals or services by lay preachers and cantors, the cantors separated from the Church as teachers - the ordinance of the Reichsstatthalter, Gustav reports, the neighbouring parishes strained since the summer) lie behind the brother's crises; it quotes Romans 8:35-39 and reads in the letters, under all the declarations of loyalty to the Führer, "a power above them to which this soldier gave himself wholly: God."

The front routine of 27 January 1943 (the snowstorms unknown in the Wartheland, the hoped-for relief into the rear, "maybe then my leave will begin, and when I return from leave, after your wedding, it will be warm and light; then the great offensives will begin and the war - God's grace willing - will end. And how is your wedding? Have you decided to go to Erika?"). Gustav's letter of 28 January 1943: Bruno's savings book at the Sparkasse (4,871 marks to the end of 1942), the oath of a tenured official at Konin, the photographs developed at Poznań - and the cold news of the fallen. On 30 January 1943 the Berlin radio plays Bruckner's Seventh before the first official communiqué of Stalingrad; no possibility that the front did not hear it, and to speak of the catastrophe threatened the charge of defeatism. Yet the letter that follows is of marriage: Bruno will marry only when released from service; the girl of Trzemeszno, Elfride Fiedler, housewifely, lively, talkative, of little education ("a good thing; I do not want a wife with a higher education to instruct me unceasingly") - and the hook: she, her parents and siblings belong to the Sabbatarians; if she decides to marry him she must go over to Lutheranism before the engagement, "I have not the least desire to go to church alone"; if she does not, he breaks off at once. The answer of the 23-year-old of Trzemeszno is plain: "I am a Seventh-day Adventist... we celebrate the seventh day" - and the acquaintance ends. Then Ursula of Lipice, leading a group of the Bund Deutscher Mädel, whose two returned letters she encloses again: love had blinded her, she has returned to her old way, "I believe in the almighty God who will not allow Germany's fall; every faith directed against my beloved homeland I reject... our Führer never meant to separate the Church from the state - on the contrary! In 1933 services were made a duty for all the party's organizations. But the Church rejected it", the Church cannot have German youth, the hierarchy acts together with the enemy states against the Reich, and when victory is won the matter with the Church will be settled - "you have sincere faith, but you have reason too, which lets you discern the future; formerly you sat in your village cut off from the events of the world."

Stalingrad and its shock (the generals Strecker and Groscurth ending their report not with Heil Hitler but "Long live Germany"); the reserve weeks of February 1943 ("today is the first Sunday - to my joy and everyone's without service... I went into the snowed-up mountains and found again an altar for prayer... I cannot tell everyone this; most would take me for a dreamer"), the propaganda's answer at the Sportpalast on 18 February 1943 (Goebbels's total-war speech before 14,000 selected guests, "Nun, Volk steh auf, und Sturm brich los!", the book edition published the same day, and Bruno's letter: "that the decision with Russia and so the end of the war will come this year we all feel; personal matters must now be set aside; when all is over there will be the beautiful return home and, as the crowning of joy, my wedding"). On 4 March 1943 the urgent order calls up the Volksdeutsche of the Warta Country to the 2nd battalion; Bruno is assigned to a heavy machine-gun as its operator, with the private Atze to help him - and the hoard keeps the only account of a battle in the whole correspondence ("From 12 at night (from Friday to Saturday) our heavy weapons were made ready... it is unbelievable how everything roars, seethes, boils and bubbles, and when the shells whistle over to the other side carrying death and destruction. Again - as always - there were many fallen and wounded on both sides (among the Russians many more)... the Russian prisoners testified that in those very days the Russians planned an attack on our positions; only we forestalled them. Yet one feels so wonderfully God's care and love").

On the day of remembrance, 21 March 1943, no leave yet, the Russian's silence since 15 March read as exhaustion ("as Hermann Göring announces, the enemy is fighting with his last reserves; and we, by the totalization of the war, can still put one more army in the field; therefore we are all firmly convinced that the Lord will send us victory this summer and grant peace to the poor people on both sides"). The letter of April 1943 to Gustav asks how "total war" has affected their life, whether the brother means to volunteer - though so needed at Łazińsk, and with the wedding in prospect (the Wehrmacht will soon decide without asking Gustav's opinion) - and reports the Führer's speech of two weeks before: "In this special spring day, when we have happily survived the winter and countless dangers, we should rejoice and be thankful that God through our Führer preserves us from the threatening evil, and how it strengthens us soldiers, that we do not bear our sacrifices, do not suffer and - die - in vain." Six days later the tone is different: no leave for Easter, "I long already for quiet, for the blessed hours... Łazińsk, Zagórów, also Anielewo, Białobłoty, Maślaki, Konary, Grodziec - all these are blessed places!"; the decisive attacks must soon swell in the east; his counsel that they listen and proclaim the holy word in the time of Pascha, which he now lacks so sorely; so they will arm themselves best for the times of drought that may come."

Then a silence in the hoard until the letter of 27 July 1943 - the book fills it with Kursk (5 July to the end of August 1943, Citadel, the greatest tank battle in history, after which the German command never regained the strategic initiative in the east): "With us it is comparatively quiet... confirmation that the Russians are using all their forces in the south to win back the central areas. Here it is often gloomy and misty. Then it is dangerous, for the Russians like to attack then; but we are on our guard and our machines do not fail." His thoughts run to Łazińsk, where the people can quietly gather the harvest; he thanks sister Anna for the parcel and tells her he is no longer writing to Elfride - "not recklessness or indifference, but rather responsibility"; on Sunday 8 August 1943, in the blessed hour of the services, he writes in a religious exaltation ("In spirit I see in all countries the temples"), seeing in them those made his siblings through the blood and salvation of Christ, sees himself in the pulpit in the most splendid of all official garments, and instead of greetings asks them to read Psalm 23 - which stands printed whole in the book.

The letter of 16 September 1943, dated "in the field" - road-building, nine to ten hours with pick and spade, "I am grateful that the food is good (better than last year) and that I can work for Germany and not as a prisoner of war in Russia, as has befallen many" - is chiefly his text for Gustav's 44th birthday: the 36-year-old Elza, known only by report, pure in faith, character and virtue; "you cannot set too high judgements and demands - inner worth remains more important than outward beauty"; even at her age she may still bear a few children. The year's dark news behind it: Sicily landed on 10 July, the Fascist Grand Council deposing Mussolini on 25 July, Italy's capitulation of 3 September, the Duce rescued by German commandos - which fills Bruno with admiration ("It pleases me especially the loyalty of our Führer. This matter in Italy will at least become clear and further steps will certainly soon be taken"); Mussolini's republic of Salò. And Gustav's answer from Łazińsk reads the Poles' changed bearing ("One can rage that the Poles are becoming impudent; all the same I would ask you to confine yourself to quiet observing and reporting; provocative intrusion breeds hatred, and hatred is capable of much. Let the gendarmerie see to the malefactors, it is called to it. The Poles rejoice in vain for political freedom. The Germans are in form!") - and sends as a birthday present a drinking glass made of a cartridge case fired at the Eastern Front in Russia.

The later letter of Gustav Adolf of 12 December 1944 (field post 33 977, by then an artilleryman of the naval infantry at Hamburg) gives his sister instructions for the Polish girl assigned to the farm as a slave: "First you must take her sharply in hand, so that she knows her place. You must lock everything up and allot everything to her; one does not know whether she does not steal and is in league with the farmhand" - with a swineherding manual and the warning not to wait with the pig-killing lest the girl and the farmhand steal the pig from the sty. (The note 29 adds that the letters of Bruno and Gustav contain the seeking out of richer Polish farmsteads to take over, and instructions on "keeping the Polish slaves briefly".)

The forged document: a hoax of the underground's information and propaganda service of the Home Army (AK), planted among the Germans - the "Reichsstelle für Familienzuwachs" of Berlin, 15 May 1943, file I.A.4711, "Concerning the fight against ruin (of the nation)": the recipient is appointed a reproducer "to serve 9 women and 18 girls" for the birth statistics, his wife without the right of divorce, promotion to "officer reproducer" with the order for copulation first class with red ribbon for a second district, extra food rations - signed "Hüpfauf". (Probably the neighbourhood knew that Gustav Adolf had long been looking for a wife.) The book notes the RuSHA's selection among the slave labourers sent to Germany.

The autumn and winter of 1943-44 from Finland: the field post number 31 059 of the 136th Gebirgsjäger Regiment; the birthday money and the jar of little bouquets of berries found between snow and ice; 8 November 1943 the tenth anniversary of the mother's death (she died in 1933) - the Catholic field mass ("there too one can hear a worthwhile word"), the wood, the Gospel of the Sunday ("many are called, but few are chosen", Matthew 22:14); the letters to Gustav (the deferment, "as a teacher Gustav can do more for the community on the spot than as a recruit"; the lessons twice a week, the teaching of German to the weak, the library of 500 volumes he runs); the Feldpost-Bücher and the Tornisterschriften (Orłowski's Literatura w III Rzeszy, Der Posener Türmer printed by the NS-Gauverlag Wartheland for the mayor of Poznań for Christmas 1943/44; "the individual is nothing!... obedience and fidelity unto death"); the course of the medics he volunteers for ("the medical service is not easy and no less dangerous in battle, for it must be in front and dress the wounded - but is all the more beautiful... I have a very strong faith"); the stolen safety pins of the medical bag he asks home to replace so as not to have to report the theft; the field post's machinery (the OKW's care for morale, the weight and formats strictly kept, the post reaching the battalion and divided to the companies).

The Christmas of 1943 from "my snug medical room": no leave at Christmas (the queue of the older men; maybe January, "which may mean a long cold journey, but others also travel in winter alive there and back, so I shall probably endure it too"); the two current correspondents (a pretty and intelligent neighbour from Konary who is not a believer, and a Volksdeutsche from Wallensen who writes "a little unintelligently"; "but one thing is certain for me: I shall not marry before I find a believing girl"); the comparison with the comrades in the south ("fifty per cent better and more beautiful"); the commander's word that "the front from the Arctic Ocean to Italy can at any moment become open" - and the gift home of Der Weg des Glaubens, sent from Hamburg. The commander knew what he was saying: in January 1944 the Red Army lifted the siege of Leningrad (27 January 1944), Army Group North withdrew to Lake Peipus, Mielke's unit among it; in the south the liberation of Ukraine, Volhynia and the Crimea; Teheran at the turn of 1943.

The letters of 1944: 2 March ("after a heavy week at the post we have, by God's kindness, quiet days so far; every day is like a feast, like a present. Only hold out until Easter, and we shall have the winter behind us. Perhaps the next one we shall have peace already"); 7 March interrupted by the alarm ("we must move; hard days are coming again"; the letter reached Łazińsk 23 March 1944, by field post 31 059E - the 136th regiment of the 2nd Gebirgs Division, 10th company); 12 March, reaching Łazińsk in five days by the field post ("How once more God's kindness has crowned me, that he has granted me (us) a free and quiet Sunday... and join the invisible prayerful community in heaven and on earth"; the cross of Golgotha letting sinners lay down their burdens - "the soldier Mielke grants himself full absolution"); the five-fingered gloves he asks for (he has two-fingered ones, so his hands do not freeze); the writing twice a week when the situation is tense; the move 70 km to the rear ("The barracks are spacious and airy. For a whole week now we have been papering the walls and working at making them beautiful... Outside there is a thaw and in some places last year's moss is showing"). On 20 April 1944, the Führer's birthday, the promotion to corporal (Obergefreiter) - "after two years of service that is nothing great, but dear to the heart all the same"; his first service as a corporal held in the melting snow, a tuft of moss for the altar ("That hour in solitude lets one see one's weaknesses"); the shame of sitting in the north listening to the pines while his comrades fight in the south ("Compared with them we are here on holiday" - "may it not get worse"); the company commander Oberleutnant Hengl, son of the lieutenant-general Ritter von Hengl commanding the 2nd Gebirgs Division (note 21: Georg Ritter von Hengl, the First World War flyer with ten English planes, the knight of the Military Order of Max Joseph, commander of the 2nd Gebirgs Division 1943 and of the XIX Mountain Corps in the period of the letters, taken prisoner in Norway in May 1945 - from Wikipedia).

And the girls: "lost" to Anna Steinbart, his hopes now on Elizabeth Kaschuba ("not plain, educated, an excellent housewife" - where did he have this from?), Gustav urged on with Erika, the double chevron of the corporal. The letter of 4 May 1944, by air (field post 48 341, the 67th Medical Company of the 2nd Gebirgs Division), tells that Bruno Mielke had been on leave at Łazińsk - he could therefore have left part of the letters that reached him at the front. It is the letter of the brother's soul: Gustav had received the Lord's Supper at Easter (note 22 explains the Lutheran Eucharist), overcome himself to strong fidelity to his God after long hindrance; "It makes me happy also because I can enter well into your situation and understand you and your needs." There was a time when the brother's departure from the Church aroused his great, oppressive care; on leave they had spoken of it with the father, who spoke anxiously of his elder son "with unspeakable sadness". "Papa despite his many errors and weaknesses is a dear soul! I am so grateful to my Lord that I still have him"; the younger son's patronizing note towards the father. Now the care turns to sister Anni, long unseen in church: "Is that not a sign of her doubtful inner state? Is it not the first sad fruit of 'Germania' with the spirit and 'religion' taken over from Hans?" The book takes the question into its longest stretch of commentary: nazism as a political religion, the völkisch primacy of race and nation, the criticism of Christianity as "not a religion of the sword" (Natalia Stawarz's Wikipedia piece, notes 23 and 26), the Deutsche Christen, the Bible scholars proving Christ an Aryan - and Gustav's own letter of 1 May 1942 as its fruit: "Should wise men then at all have lived and held God back and said: What are you doing, choose a Saviour from the German people and not from among the Jews. But it pleased God so" - written when in Zagórów and the neighbourhood there was no longer a single Jew; and Gustav's ciphered question "g. J." - gegen Juden, against the Jews (note 24: the interpreter Jacek Kin's reading, which the author holds justified by the hoard and the cantor's other utterances); Orłowski on the brown poets ("The scale of irrationalism, brutality, servility and cultishness..."); Hitler as the Lord's anointed, the faithful dead as martyrs. Bruno rejects the new religion with the full force of a believing Christian ("We gladly want to do everything for the Führer and the fatherland, but to remain a traitor and Judas to ourselves and our conscience and the Lord of all lords - that is something no one can demand, and no reasonable man (certainly also the Führer) will demand it. If they do not want us as we are, let them 'release' us. Better to follow that simple, ordinary life than to remain with a broken conscience and without moral support in this bloody, serious period!"); he congratulates Gustav for remaining faithful to his faith despite the honouring with important offices - "we already fought in the difficult period of Poland, and woe to us if we depart from our so clearly marked way. The decision therefore lies on the other side: whether they will let believing people work, or whether they want to be rid of them" (they chose the second: from another letter Gustav was soon called up to the navy); "Before the war, in the difficult period of Poland, we remained in the faith, whereas in the young Warta Country everyone gulped down the 'new fame'. They abandoned it and departed far." The book marks the two languages of the letters: the biblical diction of the personal and confessional passages, the ready clichés of the Third Reich's language (LTI) of the declarations of loyalty; and the passage where Bruno prepares his family "for the worst" - the taking of the Warta Country by the Red Army ("How will they, poorest of you, then be treated by the liberated Poles!"), the prayer to forgive those whom their own conduct had injured, the shudder at remembering that he had once urged his brother to move to Konin ("It is God's grace that in this time sliding towards destruction we have this quiet island"; "may you live in Łazińsk many sunny and happy days") - and the book's weighing: the alienation, the eksterytorialność of the land that fed them; the neighbours made slaves, the patriots killed, the houses and land plundered, and still the faith that the sunny land would be kept; the believing soldier who fights in the first line and kills, hard, no weaker than his comrades - "another matter is whether the light that shone for him was to the end bright."

The last preserved letter is dated 14 May 1944 in Norway (the same field post 48 341, the Luftfeldpost stamps on the envelope) - written after the transfer northwards; three months later Finland ceased fighting (4 September 1944) and signed the armistice of 19 September, its troops taking part in the operations against the Germans withdrawing from Lapland to Norway; from 15 September the Finns fought on the Allies' side; in October the Petsamo-Kirkenes operation drove the German 20th Mountain Army out. Bruno writes: "How it will be for me here, and how far my wishes will be fulfilled here, remains in God's hands. His will brought me here; to His guidance I want to go on entrusting myself." Transferred suddenly to a medical company, he writes on the Sunday afternoon; the last sentences of the 33-year-old that have reached us show a man who sees the whole tragedy of the war, and a muffled trace of something stirring in his conscience: the two small fair Norwegian girls coming shyly to the soldiers' kitchen with a vessel, the roll of sweets given to the younger, who like her sister wore a little case with a Christ's cross on her neck ("That child I would not want to see again! (I prayed quietly about it)"). A wide search in Polish and German sources on the net for his further fate brought nothing; the letter of 14 May 1944 is the last material trace he left. "You walk in darkness, and like a coat of night is your unknowing" - the rabbi's words to Father Józef Suryn in Iwaszkiewicz's Mother Joan of the Angels (note 27). In the war's last year the 2nd Gebirgs Division went from Norway to Denmark, fought the Western Allies at Trier and Philippsburg-Heilbronn, and ended the war partly in Württemberg, partly capitulating in the Tyrol (note 28, from Wikipedia).

The acknowledgements (p. 93) name the translators of the letters from the German - Lidia Antoniewicz, Aneta Gorzelańczyk, Jacek Kin (the greater part), Jolanta Łuczak, Michał Rek, Sylwia Roszak - letter by letter by date, with the consultations of Anna Eicke and Günter Hennings; the complete collection of the originals with the translations is kept in the archive of the MGOK at Zagórów. [The abbreviation as the book gives it.]

The appendix (pp. 95-101): "Łazińsk - the village's history is more than 280 years old", a note from Der Heimatbote 8/81-3 of the Kartoteka Wartheland, translated by Jacek Kin - the German-era account: Łazińsk a village of the former Konin powiat, almost wholly German; the way from Konin south-westwards to the gmina of Drommin (Trąbczyn), to which, besides Michalinów, the settlement of Łazińsk belonged, inhabited by about 170 German families to 1945; the year 1718, when fourteen German families came from Silesia with their village headman at their head and received from the owner of the Trąbczyn estate a great stretch of forest to make fruitful; the village grown "from a green root" (aus grüner Wurzel); the families Kuhn, Merk, Schönfisch, Haupt, met with in the neighbourhood to 1945 and on the ancestors' tablet of the Weber/Rhytthammer family; in 1968 the settlement could have celebrated its 250 years had history gone otherwise; the cemetery on the rising ground left of the kantoral school, its first grave of 1727, the weathered wooden and iron grave-stones standing to 1945; the colonists' early school and house of prayer, Łazińsk with its 150 inhabitants the largest kantorat of the later gmina of Zagórów (Hinterberg); the cantor who not only taught but held the Sunday services; to 1933 teaching and services in the old building, then under the then teacher and cantor [Gustav] Mielke the new building serving as school and house of prayer, the Polish authorities letting him work four years before transferring him to Galicia for his zeal in cultivating Germandom.
